Welcome to SIBOAT

What is SIBOAT?

SIBOAT — SiBOT, Inspired Binning of On-surface Aquatic Trash

An automated aquatic waste recovery and classification system designed to collect floating waste from calm inland waters and support on-board classification and sorting.

RESEARCH PROJECT

About SIBOAT

Download SIBOAT Android App

You can download SIBOAT directly on your Android phone.

Android phones can use either the web version or the Android app. iPhone, iPad, and other devices that do not run Android can only use the web version of SIBOAT.

Design, Development, and Evaluation of SIBOAT: An Automated Aquatic Trash Collection and Classification System

SIBOAT (SiBOT, Inspired Binning of On-surface Aquatic Trash) is an original developmental research project. It centers on a stationary, anchored machine that collects floating trash from inland waterways and automatically sorts it into categories on board, addressing a gap in most existing aquatic cleanup devices, which collect waste but don't classify it.

Research Information

Bantayan Island's fishing and freshwater supply depend on clean surrounding waters, but floating garbage threatens both. Republic Act No. 9003 requires local government units to manage solid waste, yet island municipalities often lack the budget and equipment to extend that mandate to their shorelines. Most existing cleanup devices only collect trash without sorting it, leaving segregation to be done by hand afterward. SIBOAT was developed to close that gap with a low-cost, stationary automated system.

This study set out to design, develop, and evaluate an automated aquatic waste recovery and classification system. Specifically, it aimed to define the system's mechanical, hardware, and software specifications, measure its collection efficiency, classification accuracy, and reliability, gauge its acceptability to experts and end-users, and compare its sorting speed against manual segregation, while documenting the technical challenges met along the way.

The prototype is built as a twin-hull catamaran, with an EPS foam floatation hull, a wood-and-bamboo skeleton frame, and PVC side panels to keep water out. An ESP32 microcontroller runs every subsystem, powered by a 12-volt battery that a solar panel keeps charged through the day. SIBOAT is designed to operate anchored at a fixed point, though its twin motors and paddle wheels also let an operator reposition it toward where trash is collecting, using differential thrust for steering.

Floating debris is pulled from the water onto the machine by a conveyor system driven by a 24-volt DC motor and motor driver. The intake is sized for debris up to about 1 kilogram and 30 centimeters across, which covers the plastic bottles, thin plastics, and natural debris that make up most floating waste in local waterways. Anything heavier, larger, or submerged falls outside what the prototype is built to handle.

An ESP32-CAM module and a computer vision algorithm identify each piece of collected waste as a plastic bottle, thin plastic, or natural solid debris. Two servo-actuated flaps then divert it into the matching compartment of a three-category mesh bin, so materials arrive already sorted instead of needing to be separated by hand afterward.

This dashboard communicates with the ESP32 through the user's phone hotspot. The ESP32 joins the hotspot in Wi-Fi Station mode and is addressed automatically at 10.90.102.50, with siboat.local advertised through mDNS. On the configured hotspot subnet the Main ESP32 uses 10.90.102.50; the firmware can fall back to DHCP on other subnets. HTTP is used for REST commands and health checks, while WebSocket is used for low-latency joystick and telemetry traffic when available.

Floating garbage degrades water quality, blocks natural flow, and breaks down into microplastics that move up the food chain to people and animals. By automating collection and sorting, SIBOAT is meant to give local government units, waste and recycling operators, and coastal communities a lower-cost alternative to manual cleanup, while feeding pre-sorted material back into recycling more easily than mixed waste can.

CONNECTION PROCESS

Connect to SIBOAT

Follow these steps before pressing Connect to SIBOAT.

PRIMARY SIBOAT WI-FI
SSID 1. SIBOAT NETWORKPrimary connection shown to users

Connect to SIBOAT NETWORK. The Wi-Fi password is not shown in the app; ask the SIBOAT developers/researchers for the current password. The Main ESP32 and ESP32-CAM also contain hidden fallback profiles that are not displayed here.

1
Open the connection guide

You are here. Keep this guide available while preparing the phone connection.

2
Scan the QR code

Use your phone's camera or Wi-Fi QR scanner to scan the code above.

3
Join SIBOAT NETWORK

Connect this device to SIBOAT NETWORK. The password is intentionally not displayed in the app; ask the SIBOAT developers/researchers for the current password.

4
Return to SIBOAT

Return to this web app after the phone reports that the Wi-Fi connection is established.

5
Press CONNECT TO SIBOAT

The app will verify the ESP32 over HTTP and then WebSocket. An IP address is normally not needed; use the manual IP fallback when mDNS/static discovery is unavailable.

6
Wait for the result

If successful, the status changes to CONNECTED. If it fails, the attempt stops and the app waits for you to press Connect again.

7
If there is an error

Confirm that you are still connected to SIBOAT NETWORK and that the ESP32 is powered on. Then return to Connections and press CONNECT TO SIBOAT again.

Important: Use SIBOAT NETWORK for the normal user connection. The Main ESP32 and ESP32-CAM automatically try their hidden fallback Wi-Fi profiles only when an earlier configured network is unavailable.
